data.title: Salicylic acid peel
data.summary: Lipophilic superficial peel for acne, oily skin and PIH; safe in skin types IV–V
data.body:
Salicylic acid (SA) is a lipophilic beta-hydroxy acid. It dissolves in sebum, so it works well in the follicle and on oily, acne-prone skin. Clinic strength is usually 20–30% in an ethanol base. It is a superficial peel, comedolytic and mildly anti-inflammatory, and among the safest peels for Indian skin.

## Indications
- Comedonal and mild–moderate inflammatory acne
- Post-acne PIH, oily skin, enlarged pores
- Superficial melasma and facial melanoses (adjunct to topical therapy)
- Rough photo-damaged texture, keratosis pilaris (body)

## Contraindications
- Salicylate (aspirin) allergy
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Active infection at the site: herpes labialis, impetigo, warts, open wounds
- Eczema, dermatitis or recent sunburn at the site
- Unrealistic expectations or poor sun-protection compliance
- Large-area peels in renal or hepatic disease (salicylism risk)

## Pre-procedure
- Written consent: expected stinging, dryness, flaking, and possible PIH
- Counsel that 4–6 sessions are needed and results are gradual
- **Priming 2–4 weeks**: broad-spectrum sunscreen + 2–4% hydroquinone or azelaic acid ± tretinoin 0.025% at night
- Stop retinoids and scrubs 3–5 days before; no waxing or threading for 1 week
- Herpes history: start acyclovir/valacyclovir on the day of the peel
- Test patch behind the ear or on the jawline before the first full peel
- Clinical photographs in standard lighting

## Equipment
- SA 20% and 30% solution, gloves, gauze, cotton-tipped applicators
- Cleanser, alcohol or acetone for degreasing
- Petrolatum for the nasal alae, lip commissures and inner canthi
- Hand-held fan, timer, cool water, ice packs

## Procedure step by step
1. Cleanse the face and degrease with alcohol or acetone; let it dry.
2. Protect the eyes; apply petrolatum to the alar creases, commissures and canthi.
3. Apply the first coat quickly and evenly with gauze: forehead, cheeks, nose, chin, then perioral.
4. Expect burning for 1–2 minutes, then a relative numbness from the anaesthetic effect of SA; use the fan.
5. **Endpoint**: an even white crystalline precipitate (pseudofrost) with mild erythema, usually at 3–5 minutes. This is salicylic acid crystallising, not protein coagulation.
6. A second coat can be applied to oily or acne-prone areas in later sessions.
7. Neutralisation is not required (the peel is self-limiting). Wash off with plain water after 3–5 minutes.
8. Apply a bland moisturiser and sunscreen before the patient leaves.

## Post-procedure care
- Gentle cleanser, plain moisturiser, SPF 30+ reapplied every 3 hours outdoors
- Do not pick or peel the flakes; mild flaking lasts 2–4 days
- Restart priming agents after 3–5 days once the skin is calm

## Complications & management
- Excess erythema or burning: cool compresses, mid-potency topical steroid for 2–3 days
- PIH: hydroquinone or azelaic acid, strict photoprotection; space out sessions
- Acneiform flare: usually settles with continued treatment
- Herpes reactivation: treatment-dose antiviral
- Salicylism (tinnitus, nausea, dizziness) with large areas: stop and wash off; avoid body peels over large surfaces

## Sessions & follow-up
- Every 2–3 weeks for 4–6 sessions; start at 20% and step up to 30% if tolerated
- Review the photographs at each visit; continue maintenance topicals between sessions
